# Functional Programming - Writing Reusable Code

## Load libraries
```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(tibble)
library(palmerpenguins)
library(PNWColors)
```

## Functions
Use a function when:

You have a task you want to use more than once You want to keep your script clean and organized You want to avoid mistakes with copy and paste You minimize places where you need to update your code

### Rescaling data

#### Random

```{r}
df <- tibble(
  a = rnorm(10), # rnorm means random number
  b = rnorm(10),
  c = rnorm(10),
  d = rnorm(10)
)

head(df)
```

#### Manual

```{r}
df <- df |>
  mutate(a = (a - min(a, na.rm = TRUE)) / (max(a, na.rm = TRUE) - min(a, na.rm = TRUE)))

head(df)
```

#### Writing a function

Create a reusable rescaling function

```{r}
rescale01 <- function(x) {
  value <- (x - min(x, na.rm = TRUE)) / (max(x, na.rm = TRUE) - min(x, na.rm = TRUE))
  return(value)
}

df |>
  mutate(
    a = rescale01(a),
    b = rescale01(b),
    c = rescale01(c),
    d = rescale01(d)
  )
```

Even better, use mutate(across(everything())). Much cleaner! One line rescales all columns.

```{r}
df |>
  mutate(across(everything(), rescale01))
```

**Anatomy of a function** 

1. Function name 
2. Arguments: related to what is going in, lists the inputs 
3. Function body: the {} block containng the code 
4. Return statement: what the function returns

##### Examples

**F to C** 
Step 1: The conversion formula

```{r}
temp_C <- (temp_F -32) * 5 /9

```

Step 2: Step 2: Create the function structure

```{r}
f_to_celsius <- function() {# code goes here}
```

Step 3

```{r}
f_to_celsius <- function() {
  temp_C <- (temp_F - 32) * 5 / 9
}
```

Step 4

```{r}
f_to_celsius <- function(temp_F) {
  temp_C <- (temp_F - 32) * 5 / 9
}
```

Step 5

```{r}
f_to_celsius <- function(temp_F) {
  temp_C <- (temp_F - 32) * 5 / 9
  return(temp_C)
}
```

try plotting any temp

```{r}
f_to_celsius(32)
```

**K to C**

```{r}
c_to_k <- function(temp_celsius) {
  temp_K <- (temp_celsius+273.15)
  return(temp_K)
}
```

## Making Plot Functions

### Why turn plots into functions?

If you have a plot format you use repeatedly, create a function to:

- Write it once, use it many times
- Maintain consistency across figures
- Save time and reduce errors

Let’s create a reusable plot function with the penguin dataset:

```{r}
pal <- pnw_palette("Lake", 3, type = "discrete")

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = body_mass_g, y = bill_length_mm, color = island)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  scale_color_manual("Island", values = pal) +
  theme_bw()
```

### Name and set up the function

```{r}
myplot <- function(data, x, y) {
  pal <- pnw_palette("Lake", 3, type = "discrete")
  
  ggplot(data, aes(x = x, y = y, color = island)) +
    geom_point() +
    geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
    scale_color_manual("Island", values = pal) +
    theme_bw()
}
```

```{r}
myplot(data = penguins, x = body_mass_g, y = bill_length_mm)
```

Use curly-curly {{}} for column names

```{r}
myplot <- function(data, x, y) {
  pal <- pnw_palette("Lake", 3, type = "discrete")
  
  ggplot(data, aes(x = {{x}}, y = {{y}}, color = island)) +
    geom_point() +
    geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
    scale_color_manual("Island", values = pal) +
    theme_bw()
}
```

Test

```{r}
myplot(data = penguins, x = flipper_length_mm, y = bill_length_mm)
```

#### Default arguments

```{r}
myplot <- function(data = penguins, x, y) { # like na.rm defalult is TRUE
  pal <- pnw_palette("Lake", 3, type = "discrete")
  
  ggplot(data, aes(x = {{x}}, y = {{y}}, color = island)) + # can add {{}} around color=color if want to use that too
    geom_point() +
    geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
    scale_color_manual("Island", values = pal) +
    theme_bw()
}
```

Now you can call it with just the column arguments:

```{r}
myplot(x = body_mass_g, y = flipper_length_mm)
```

#### Layer onto the function

```{r}
myplot(x = body_mass_g, y = flipper_length_mm) +
  labs(x = "Body mass (g)", y = "Flipper length (mm)")
```

## Adding control flow with if-else

### The if-else statement

Use if-else to execute different code based on a condition:

```{r}
a <- 6 # assign values
b <- 5

if (a > b) { # has to be true or false answer
  f <- 20 # bracket is output
} else { # if answer if false, then the output
  f <- 10
}

f # test output
```

#### Making your function more flexible

Add an argument to toggle features on/off:

```{r}
myplot <- function(data = penguins, x, y, lines = TRUE) { # default is true/on
  pal <- pnw_palette("Lake", 3, type = "discrete")
  
  if (lines == TRUE) { # EXACTLY EQUAL TO 
    ggplot(data, aes(x = {{x}}, y = {{y}}, color = island)) +
      geom_point() +
      geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
      scale_color_manual("Island", values = pal) +
      theme_bw()
  } else {
    ggplot(data, aes(x = {{x}}, y = {{y}}, color = island)) +
      geom_point() + # no geom smooth if FALSE
      scale_color_manual("Island", values = pal) +
      theme_bw()
  }
}
```

Test w lines (default)

```{r}
myplot(x = body_mass_g, y = flipper_length_mm)
```

Test w/o lines

```{r}
myplot(x = body_mass_g, y = flipper_length_mm, lines = FALSE)
```
